newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan ruling LDP mulls stock boosting steps.
newsitem.headline: Japan ruling LDP mulls stock boosting steps.

text.p: Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) is mulling steps such as scrapping unpopular taxes on securities transactions as a way to prop up the nation's fragile stock market, party officials said on Wednesday.

Worried that the recent stock plunge has darkened prospects for corporate earnings in the business year to March, lawmakers have started to urge the government to scrap a securities transaction tax which brokers complain dampens share trade.
A member of the LDP's tax research council told Reuters on Wednesday that Japan should abolish the securities transaction tax as early as 1998.

"Given our policy task of carrying out "Big Bang" financial reforms and putting Japan's securities market on an international footing, we must consider abolishing the securities transaction tax, because there are no such tax systems abroad," said the official, who declined to be named.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last November unveiled a five-year "Big Bang" programme to liberalise Japan's financial markets and catch up with Western nations by the year 2001.
The LDP's tax advisory panel is likely to start discussing how to carry out tax reforms earlier than the autumn, when the council usually kicks off such debate, he said.
Hopes the government may scrap taxes on securities tradings energised sagging Japanese stocks on Wednesday, driving the key market barometer up nearly four percent by the end of the day.
The 225-share Nikkei average surged 655.72 points, or 3.78 percent, clearing the key 18,000 threshold to end at 18,013.88.
Oppoisiton parties are likely to join the LDP's effort to cheer up sagging Tokyo stocks.

Ichiro Ozawa, head of the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), told Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in parliament on Wednesday that Japan must scrap the securities transaction tax as well as continue special income tax cuts which Hashimoto has said will not be implemented this year.
Ozawa also blasted the government's half-hearted efforts to carry out structural reforms in the economy.

A key advisory panel to the finance minister could unveil proposals for steps such as the liberalisation of brokerage commissions and the abolition or easing of securities taxes before end-March, instead of June when the panel was originally scheduled to make such proposals, another LDP lawmaker said.

"The current stock weakness largely reflects psychological worries, because both the economy and corporate activities are now picking up. In order to cope with the situation, it is necessary for the government to show its strong resolve to pursue 'Big Bang' financial reforms," the lawmaker said.

Market participants also hope to see more tax reforms, especially of land taxes, which could help financial institutions bogged down by property-related bad loans and free up funds for the real estate market. Land tax reform would also bolster Japan's timid economic recovery, analysts said.

LDP officials, however, remain reluctant to take such steps as the resumption of special income tax cuts or changes in property taxes because doing so would require a revision in next fiscal year's budget, now under parliamentary discussion.
LDP lawmakers are also reluctant to seek any extra public spending to help banks write off their bad loan holdings.
